claim: 145 HML-2-like proviruses were identified in rhesus macaques.

evidence: This is an inference drawn from multiple lines of data presented in the manuscript including LTR divergence analysis, ORF identification, and PCR screening.

claim: 106 of the rhesus HML-2-like proviruses form a clade characterized by an ~750 bp sequence between env and the 3′ LTR.
source: 106 of the proviruses form a clade characterized by an ~750 bp sequence between env and the 3′ long terminal repeat (LTR), derived from an ancient recombination with a HERV-K(HML-8)-related virus.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the structural and phylogenetic analysis reported in the manuscript.

claim: The ~750 bp sequence between env and the 3′ LTR in 106 rhesus proviruses is derived from an ancient recombination with a HERV-K(HML-8)-related virus.
source: 106 of the proviruses form a clade characterized by an ~750 bp sequence between env and the 3′ long terminal repeat (LTR), derived from an ancient recombination with a HERV-K(HML-8)-related virus.
evidence: This is an inference based on sequence homology analysis showing the region has ~85% nucleotide identity to MER11A elements (HML-8 LTRs).

claim: The recombinant clade is found in Old World monkeys (OWM) but not great apes.
source: This clade is found in Old World monkeys (OWM), but not great apes, suggesting it originated after the ape/OWM split.
evidence: This is based on BLAT searches of multiple primate genomes reported in the manuscript.

claim: The recombinant clade originated after the ape/OWM split.
source: This clade is found in Old World monkeys (OWM), but not great apes, suggesting it originated after the ape/OWM split.
evidence: This is an inference based on the phylogenetic distribution of the recombinant proviruses.

claim: Similar recombinant proviruses were identified in white-cheeked gibbons.
source: We identified similar proviruses in white-cheeked gibbons; the gibbon insertions cluster within the OWM recombinant clade, suggesting interspecies transmission from OWM to gibbons.
evidence: This is a primary finding from genome mining and phylogenetic analysis.

claim: The gibbon insertions cluster within the OWM recombinant clade.

claim: The LTRs of the youngest proviruses have deletions in U3 which disrupt the Rec Response Element (RcRE).

claim: The Rec Response Element (RcRE) is required for nuclear export of unspliced viral RNA.

claim: The HML-8-derived region functions as a Rec-independent constitutive transport element (CTE).
source: We show that the HML-8-derived region functions as a Rec-independent constitutive transport element (CTE), indicating the ancestral Rec–RcRE export system was replaced by a CTE mechanism.
evidence: This is demonstrated experimentally using the dual reporter assay shown in Figure 7 and the MPMV infection assay shown in Figure 8.

claim: The ancestral Rec–RcRE export system was replaced by a CTE mechanism in SERV-K/MER11.

claim: Retroviruses must irreversibly integrate their genome into the host genome in order to replicate.
source: Uniquely among animal viruses, they must irreversibly integrate their genome into the host genome in order to replicate (Brown, 1997; Hughes et al., 1978).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: If an infected germline cell survives, the provirus may be inherited by offspring as a heterozygous allele.
source: if a germline cell is infected, the provirus may be inherited by an offspring of the host organism as a heterozygous allele, which may eventually become fixed in the descendant population (Stoye, 2012).
evidence: This is established knowledge about ERV biology supported by citation.

claim: Approximately 8% of the human genome is composed of endogenous retrovirus sequences.
source: Such proviruses and remnants of such proviruses, known as endogenous retroviruses (ERVs), form a major fraction of most eukaryotic genomes; in humans, ~8% of the genome is composed of such sequences (Griffiths, 2001).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: No replication competent human ERV (HERV) has been identified.
source: No replication competent human ERV (HERV) has been identified; however, the betaretrovirus-like HERV-K group contains one subgroup, human MMTV-like-2, or HML-2 (named for its similarity to mouse mammary tumor virus (MMTV)), which includes many proviruses with full-length open reading frames (ORFs) and other intact functional elements, including two proviruses with full-length ORFs for the four core retroviral proteins Gag, Pro, Pol, and Env (Boller et al., 2008; Hanke et al., 2016; Subramanian et al., 2011; Wildschutte et al., 2016).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: HML-2 includes two proviruses with full-length ORFs for the four core retroviral proteins Gag, Pro, Pol, and Env.
source: No replication competent human ERV (HERV) has been identified; however, the betaretrovirus-like HERV-K group contains one subgroup, human MMTV-like-2, or HML-2 (named for its similarity to mouse mammary tumor virus (MMTV)), which includes many proviruses with full-length open reading frames (ORFs) and other intact functional elements, including two proviruses with full-length ORFs for the four core retroviral proteins Gag, Pro, Pol, and Env (Boller et al., 2008; Hanke et al., 2016; Subramanian et al., 2011; Wildschutte et al., 2016).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: The LTR5Hs subclade is the youngest HERV clade.
source: The majority of HML-2 proviruses containing full-length ORFs are within the LTR5Hs subclade, which is the youngest HERV clade and contains many human specific and insertionally polymorphic proviruses that have not yet reached fixation in human populations (Subramanian et al., 2011; Wildschutte et al., 2016).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: LTR5Hs contains many human specific and insertionally polymorphic proviruses.
source: The majority of HML-2 proviruses containing full-length ORFs are within the LTR5Hs subclade, which is the youngest HERV clade and contains many human specific and insertionally polymorphic proviruses that have not yet reached fixation in human populations (Subramanian et al., 2011; Wildschutte et al., 2016).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: A synthetic consensus young HML-2 provirus is weakly replication competent.
source: Although none of these proviruses are replication competent, two groups have shown that a synthetic consensus young HML-2 provirus is weakly replication competent, and expression of HML-2 RNA and proteins has been observed in a number of different diseases (Dewannieux et al., 2006; Garcia-Montojo et al., 2018; Goering et al., 2015; Hanke et al., 2016; Magiorkinis et al., 2013; Schmitt et al., 2013; Wang-Johanning et al., 2014; Lee and Bieniasz, 2007).

claim: The oldest known human HML-2 proviruses have orthologous insertions in both apes and Old World monkeys.
source: The oldest known human HML-2 proviruses have orthologous insertions in both apes and Old World monkeys (OWM), indicating that the clade originated in the common ancestor of the catarrhine primates (Bannert and Kurth, 2006).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: HML-2 originated in the common ancestor of the catarrhine primates.
source: The oldest known human HML-2 proviruses have orthologous insertions in both apes and Old World monkeys (OWM), indicating that the clade originated in the common ancestor of the catarrhine primates (Bannert and Kurth, 2006).
evidence: This is an inference based on phylogenetic distribution, supported by citation.

claim: HML-2 has more recently been actively replicating in gorillas than in humans.
source: A recent study reported that HML-2 has more recently been actively replicating in gorillas than in humans, though it is still unclear whether that activity has continued to the present day; some chimpanzee-specific insertions have also been identified, although fewer than in humans or gorillas (Holloway et al., 2019; Macfarlane and Badge, 2015).
evidence: This is established knowledge from a recent study, supported by citation.

claim: Orthologs of the oldest SERV-K/MER11 insertions are not found in any apes.
source: Consistent with this estimate, orthologs of the oldest insertions are found in species from both subfamilies of OWM, but not in any apes.
evidence: This is based on BLAT searches of ape genomes.

claim: 36 recombinant proviruses have identical LTRs.
source: Thirty-six of the recombinant proviruses have identical LTRs, and thus our best estimate is that they are younger than ~500,000 years old, the average time for a single nucleotide difference to occur between two 588 bp LTRs given the assumed neutral mutation rate
evidence: This is based on LTR sequence comparison.

claim: Proviruses with identical LTRs are estimated to be younger than ~500,000 years old.
source: Thirty-six of the recombinant proviruses have identical LTRs, and thus our best estimate is that they are younger than ~500,000 years old, the average time for a single nucleotide difference to occur between two 588 bp LTRs given the assumed neutral mutation rate
evidence: This is an estimate based on molecular clock calculations.

claim: The oldest SERV-K/MER11 provirus identified, 5-85732019_RM10, integrated ~25 million years ago.
source: We estimate that the oldest SERV-K/MER11 provirus identified, 5-85732019_RM10, integrated ~25 million years ago.
evidence: This is an estimate based on LTR divergence analysis.

claim: Orthologous proviral insertions of 5-85732019_RM10 are present in the genomes of both cercopithecine and colobine OWM species.
source: Consistent with this age, orthologous proviral insertions are present in the genomes of both cercopithecine and colobine OWM species, indicating that it integrated in a common ancestor of OWMs, prior to the cercopithecine-colobine split, between 9 and 26 million years ago (Finstermeier et al., 2013; Pozzi et al., 2014; Springer et al., 2012).
evidence: This is based on BLAT searches of OWM genomes.

claim: 5-85732019_RM10 integrated in a common ancestor of OWMs, prior to the cercopithecine-colobine split, between 9 and 26 million years ago.
source: Consistent with this age, orthologous proviral insertions are present in the genomes of both cercopithecine and colobine OWM species, indicating that it integrated in a common ancestor of OWMs, prior to the cercopithecine-colobine split, between 9 and 26 million years ago (Finstermeier et al., 2013; Pozzi et al., 2014; Springer et al., 2012).
evidence: This is an inference based on phylogenetic distribution and cited estimates of divergence times.

claim: 6 out of 23 screened proviruses were determined to be insertionally polymorphic in rhesus macaques.
source: 6/23 were determined to be insertionally polymorphic in rhesus macaques, with at least one individual heterozygous or homozygous for the empty site allele (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is based on allele-specific PCR screening shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: Allele frequencies for the unfixed, insertionally polymorphic proviruses ranged from 10.7 to 70.8%.
source: Allele frequencies for the unfixed, insertionally polymorphic proviruses ranged from 10.7 to 70.8%, with 14-9169782 RM10 and SERV-K1 having the lowest frequencies of the screened proviruses.
evidence: This is based on allele-specific PCR screening data.

claim: 14-9169782_RM10 and SERV-K1 have the lowest allele frequencies of the screened proviruses.
source: Allele frequencies for the unfixed, insertionally polymorphic proviruses ranged from 10.7 to 70.8%, with 14-9169782 RM10 and SERV-K1 having the lowest frequencies of the screened proviruses.
evidence: This is based on allele-specific PCR screening data.

claim: The youngest non-recombinant provirus in rhesus macaques is estimated to have integrated ~10 million years ago.
source: In contrast to SERV-K/MER11 proviruses, the non-recombinant proviruses are much older on average; the youngest non-recombinant provirus in rhesus macaques is estimated to have integrated ~10 million years ago, although orthologous insertions are present in colobine monkeys as well, suggesting that this age may be an underestimate.
evidence: This is an estimate based on LTR divergence analysis.

claim: Orthologous insertions of the youngest non-recombinant provirus are present in colobine monkeys, suggesting the age estimate may be an underestimate.
source: In contrast to SERV-K/MER11 proviruses, the non-recombinant proviruses are much older on average; the youngest non-recombinant provirus in rhesus macaques is estimated to have integrated ~10 million years ago, although orthologous insertions are present in colobine monkeys as well, suggesting that this age may be an underestimate.
evidence: This is an inference based on phylogenetic distribution.

claim: Thirteen SERV-K/MER11 insertions in total were found in all OWMs.
source: Thirteen insertions in total were found in all OWMs, but no orthologous insertions were found in ape genomes, consistent with the recombination event that formed SERV-K/MER11 occurring after the split of apes and OWMs, 20–66 million years ago, but before the cercopithecine-colobine split (Bergeron et al., 2021; Finstermeier et al., 2013; Pozzi et al., 2014; Springer et al., 2012).
evidence: This is based on BLAT searches of multiple primate genomes.

claim: No orthologous SERV-K/MER11 insertions were found in ape genomes.
source: Thirteen insertions in total were found in all OWMs, but no orthologous insertions were found in ape genomes, consistent with the recombination event that formed SERV-K/MER11 occurring after the split of apes and OWMs, 20–66 million years ago, but before the cercopithecine-colobine split (Bergeron et al., 2021; Finstermeier et al., 2013; Pozzi et al., 2014; Springer et al., 2012).
evidence: This is based on BLAT searches of ape genomes.

claim: The split of apes and OWMs occurred 20–66 million years ago.
source: Thirteen insertions in total were found in all OWMs, but no orthologous insertions were found in ape genomes, consistent with the recombination event that formed SERV-K/MER11 occurring after the split of apes and OWMs, 20–66 million years ago, but before the cercopithecine-colobine split (Bergeron et al., 2021; Finstermeier et al., 2013; Pozzi et al., 2014; Springer et al., 2012).
evidence: This is established knowledge from cited studies.

claim: Fifty-three proviruses appear to be rhesus macaque specific.
source: Fifty-three proviruses appear to be rhesus macaque specific, as no orthologous insertion is present in the crab-eating macaque reference genome; all of these proviruses cluster within either subclade 1 or 2.
evidence: This is based on BLAT searches of the crab-eating macaque genome.

claim: All rhesus macaque specific proviruses cluster within either subclade 1 or 2.
source: Fifty-three proviruses appear to be rhesus macaque specific, as no orthologous insertion is present in the crab-eating macaque reference genome; all of these proviruses cluster within either subclade 1 or 2.
evidence: This is based on phylogenetic analysis shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Nine SERV-K/MER11 proviruses were identified in the northern white-cheeked gibbon genome.
source: Although we were unable to identify any orthologues of the oldest SERV-K/MER11 insertions in ape genomes, and BLAT searches using SERV-K1 as a query confirmed the absence of similar recombinant proviruses in great apes, to our surprise, a BLAT search of the northern white-cheeked gibbon (Nomascus leucogenys) genome (Carbone et al., 2014) revealed nine proviruses, with high sequence identity to SERV-K/MER11 (Figure 4).
evidence: This is a primary finding from genome mining.

claim: Gibbon SERV-K/MER11 proviruses have the same overall structure as rhesus SERV-K/MER11.
source: These proviruses have the same overall structure as SERV-K/MER11, with short LTRs, an env with an HML-8-derived C-terminal region followed by a MER11-derived non-coding region, and a short sequence derived from the ancestral HML-2 env in between the MER11 element and the 3′ LTR, containing the PPT.
evidence: This is based on structural analysis shown in Figure 4.

claim: None of the gibbon proviruses have orthologous insertions in macaques.
source: None of the proviruses have orthologous insertions in macaques, and they cluster within the OWM SERV-K/MER11 clade in pol and LTR trees, specifically clustering with a clade of SERV-K/MER11 proviruses in the GSM genome (Figure 5A, B).
evidence: This is based on BLAT searches and phylogenetic analysis.

claim: Gibbon proviruses cluster within the OWM SERV-K/MER11 clade in pol and LTR trees.
source: None of the proviruses have orthologous insertions in macaques, and they cluster within the OWM SERV-K/MER11 clade in pol and LTR trees, specifically clustering with a clade of SERV-K/MER11 proviruses in the GSM genome (Figure 5A, B).
evidence: This is based on phylogenetic analysis shown in Figure 5A and 5B.

claim: Gibbon proviruses specifically cluster with a clade of SERV-K/MER11 proviruses in the GSM genome.
source: None of the proviruses have orthologous insertions in macaques, and they cluster within the OWM SERV-K/MER11 clade in pol and LTR trees, specifically clustering with a clade of SERV-K/MER11 proviruses in the GSM genome (Figure 5A, B).
evidence: This is based on phylogenetic analysis shown in Figure 5A and 5B.

claim: The characteristics of gibbon proviruses strongly suggest they are the result of an interspecies transmission from an OWM to an ancestral gibbon species.
source: These characteristics all strongly suggest that these proviruses are the result of an interspecies transmission from an OWM to an ancestral gibbon species.
evidence: This is an inference based on phylogenetic clustering and absence of orthologs in macaques.

claim: Four gibbon proviruses have full-length ORFs for one or more genes, with a total of 3 gag, 4 pro, and 2 env ORFs.
source: Four of the gibbon proviruses identified have full-length ORFs for one or more genes, with a total of 3 gag, 4 pro, and 2 env ORFs; no intact pol ORFs were identified (Figure 4).
evidence: This is based on ORF analysis shown in Figure 4.

claim: No intact pol ORFs were identified in gibbon proviruses.
source: Four of the gibbon proviruses identified have full-length ORFs for one or more genes, with a total of 3 gag, 4 pro, and 2 env ORFs; no intact pol ORFs were identified (Figure 4).
evidence: This is based on ORF analysis shown in Figure 4.

claim: Six gibbon proviruses have discordantly clustering 5′ and 3′ LTRs, suggestive of extensive inter-provirus recombination.
source: Six of the proviruses have discordantly clustering 5′ and 3′ LTRs, suggestive of extensive inter-provirus recombination (Figure 5B; Hughes and Coffin, 2005).
evidence: This is based on phylogenetic analysis shown in Figure 5B, with interpretation supported by citation.

claim: One gibbon provirus (10_73510506-gib) appears to be the result of an inter or intrachromosomal recombination between two proviruses, resulting in a chromosomal translocation.
source: Interestingly, one provirus with discordantly clustering LTRs, 10_73510506-gib, appears to be the result of an inter or intrachromosomal recombination between two proviruses, resulting in a chromosomal translocation; the target site duplications (TSDs) at the ends of the provirus, which should be identical, do not match each other, and the flanking sequences map to two different human chromosomes (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is an inference based on mismatched TSDs and synteny analysis shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: A solo LTR at chr10:5,132,425–5,132,933 appears to be the reciprocal recombinant locus of the chromosomal translocation.
source: We identified a solo LTR at chr10:5,132,425–5,132,933 that appears to be the reciprocal recombinant locus, with flanking sequences corresponding to the other halves of the predicted chromosomal translocation, and corresponding mismatched TSDs.
evidence: This is an inference based on synteny and TSD analysis shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: Two gibbon proviruses (2_53287052-gib and 3_145603263-gib) have estimated ages of ~1.2 and ~2.4 million years, respectively.
source: Two proviruses, 2_53287052-gib and 3_145603263-gib, had intact, non-discordant 5′ and 3′ LTRs and were thus amenable to age estimation, with estimated ages of ~1.2 and~2.4 million years, respectively, indicating that the interspecies transmission event occurred at least 2.4 million years ago.
evidence: This is an estimate based on LTR divergence analysis.

claim: The interspecies transmission event to gibbons occurred at least 2.4 million years ago.
source: Two proviruses, 2_53287052-gib and 3_145603263-gib, had intact, non-discordant 5′ and 3′ LTRs and were thus amenable to age estimation, with estimated ages of ~1.2 and~2.4 million years, respectively, indicating that the interspecies transmission event occurred at least 2.4 million years ago.
evidence: This is an inference based on the age of the oldest gibbon provirus.

claim: Gibbon SERV-K/MER11 LTRs have deletions relative to human HML-2 that overlap with but are distinct from those found in rhesus proviruses.
source: As mentioned above, the LTRs of gibbon SERV-K/MER11 have deletions relative to human HML-2, similar to those of rhesus SERV-K/MER11. These deletions overlap with those found in rhesus proviruses, but are distinct from them.
evidence: This is based on structural analysis shown in Figure 5C.

claim: Two types of gibbon proviral LTRs were identified: one with a single ~200 bp deletion (Δ4), and another with an ~370 bp deletion followed by an ~100 bp deletion (Δ5 and Δ6).
source: We identified two types of gibbon proviral LTRs: one type has a single ~200 bp deletion, Δ4, and the other type has an ~370 bp deletion followed by an ~100 bp deletion, named Δ5 and Δ6, respectively (Figure 5C).
evidence: This is based on structural analysis shown in Figure 5C.

claim: Some GSM proviruses have the same Δ4 deletion found in gibbons.
source: As previously mentioned, the closest known relatives of the gibbon SERV-K/MER11 clade are proviruses we identified in GSM; some of these proviruses have the same Δ4 deletion found in gibbons, suggesting that the viral lineage that originally crossed over into gibbons also had this deletion.
evidence: This is based on structural analysis shown in Figure 5C.

claim: The viral lineage that originally crossed over into gibbons likely had the Δ4 deletion.
source: As previously mentioned, the closest known relatives of the gibbon SERV-K/MER11 clade are proviruses we identified in GSM; some of these proviruses have the same Δ4 deletion found in gibbons, suggesting that the viral lineage that originally crossed over into gibbons also had this deletion.
evidence: This is an inference based on the shared deletion in GSM and gibbon proviruses.

claim: GSM proviruses were identified with both Δ4 and another ~180 bp deletion (Δ7).
source: In addition to GSM proviruses with a single Δ4 deletion, we identified proviruses with both Δ4 and another ~180 bp deletion, Δ7, as well as proviruses with the same Δ3 deletion found in rhesus macaques.
evidence: This is based on structural analysis shown in Figure 5C.

claim: GSM proviruses were identified with the same Δ3 deletion found in rhesus macaques.
source: In addition to GSM proviruses with a single Δ4 deletion, we identified proviruses with both Δ4 and another ~180 bp deletion, Δ7, as well as proviruses with the same Δ3 deletion found in rhesus macaques.
evidence: This is based on structural analysis shown in Figure 5C.

claim: All but one of the LTR deletions overlap with the Rec Response Element (RcRE).
source: The aforementioned LTR deletions are all found in the U3 region of the LTR. We noticed that all but one of them also overlap with the Rec Response Element (RcRE), a 433 nucleotide structured RNA element within the U3 region of human HML-2 that binds Rec, an HML-2 accessory protein that is necessary for nuclear export of unspliced and partially spliced viral mRNAs (Figure 5C; Löwer et al., 1995; Magin-Lachmann et al., 2001; Magin et al., 1999; Yang et al., 1999).
evidence: This is based on structural analysis shown in Figure 5C.

claim: The RcRE is a 433 nucleotide structured RNA element within the U3 region of human HML-2 that binds Rec.
source: The aforementioned LTR deletions are all found in the U3 region of the LTR. We noticed that all but one of them also overlap with the Rec Response Element (RcRE), a 433 nucleotide structured RNA element within the U3 region of human HML-2 that binds Rec, an HML-2 accessory protein that is necessary for nuclear export of unspliced and partially spliced viral mRNAs (Figure 5C; Löwer et al., 1995; Magin-Lachmann et al., 2001; Magin et al., 1999; Yang et al., 1999).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Rec is an HML-2 accessory protein that is necessary for nuclear export of unspliced and partially spliced viral mRNAs.
source: The aforementioned LTR deletions are all found in the U3 region of the LTR. We noticed that all but one of them also overlap with the Rec Response Element (RcRE), a 433 nucleotide structured RNA element within the U3 region of human HML-2 that binds Rec, an HML-2 accessory protein that is necessary for nuclear export of unspliced and partially spliced viral mRNAs (Figure 5C; Löwer et al., 1995; Magin-Lachmann et al., 2001; Magin et al., 1999; Yang et al., 1999).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: The LTR deletions would likely abrogate or abolish RcRE function.
source: As this RNA export process is essential for viral replication, and it seemed likely that these deletions would abrogate or abolish RcRE function, we wondered whether SERV-K/MER11 proviruses have evolved a new or altered mechanism for unspliced RNA transport.
evidence: This is an inference based on the overlap of deletions with the RcRE.

claim: SERV-K/MER11 proviruses may have evolved a new or altered mechanism for unspliced RNA transport.
source: As this RNA export process is essential for viral replication, and it seemed likely that these deletions would abrogate or abolish RcRE function, we wondered whether SERV-K/MER11 proviruses have evolved a new or altered mechanism for unspliced RNA transport.
evidence: This is speculation that motivated the experimental investigation.

claim: CTEs provide the RNA transport mechanism used by MPMV, avian leukosis virus, and some other simple retroviruses.
source: CTEs provide the RNA transport mechanism used by Mason-Pfizer monkey virus (MPMV), avian leukosis virus, and some other simple retroviruses (Bray et al., 1994; Ogert et al., 1996; Pessel-Vivares et al., 2015).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: HML-2 Rec is translated from a doubly spliced RNA with the first coding exon derived from the Env signal peptide and the second coding exon beginning near the C-terminus of Env in an alternate reading frame.
source: We first asked whether SERV-K/MER11 proviruses still make a rec-like transcript. HML-2 Rec is translated from a doubly spliced RNA; the first coding exon is derived from the Env signal peptide, and the second coding exon begins near the C-terminus of Env, in an alternate reading frame (Figure 6A).
evidence: This is established knowledge about HML-2 biology.

claim: The region containing the second rec exon has been replaced in SERV-K/MER11 by HML-8-derived sequence.
source: The region containing this exon has been replaced in SERV-K/MER11 by HML-8-derived sequence; as this region is only ~50% identical to HML-2 at the nucleotide level, we were unsure whether the rec splice form would be preserved, or make a functional protein.
evidence: This is based on structural analysis.

claim: Many RNAseq reads corresponding to a rec-like splice form were observed in rhesus macaque iPSCs, with both donor and acceptor sites matching the known rec sites.
source: As HERV-K HML-2 is known to be expressed in human embryonic stem cells and induced pluripotent stem cells (iPSCs) (Fuchs et al., 2013), we aligned a publically available rhesus macaque iPSC RNAseq dataset (Fang et al., 2014) to the SERV-K1 proviral genome using HISAT2 (Kim et al., 2019), and looked for reads crossing splice junctions of rec or other alternatively spliced RNAs using the Integrative Genomics Viewer (IGV) (Robinson et al., 2011). Despite the limited sequence similarity, we observed many reads corresponding to a rec-like splice form, with both donor and acceptor sites matching the known rec sites (Figure 6, Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is based on RNAseq analysis shown in Figure 6 and Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: The rec-like transcript is predicted to make a 149 aa protein called sRec, with the first 87 residues derived from the ancestral Rec protein and the other 62 residues encoded by HML-8-derived sequence.
source: This transcript is predicted to make a 149 aa protein, with the first 87 residues derived from the ancestral Rec protein, and the other 62 residues encoded by HML-8-derived sequence (Figure 6).
evidence: This is based on sequence analysis shown in Figure 6.

claim: The HML-2-derived exon of sRec is ~80% identical at the amino acid level to HML-2 Rec.
source: The HML-2-derived exon of this Rec-like protein, which we have called sRec, is ~80% identical at the amino acid level to HML-2 Rec; the HML-8-derived exon, in contrast, is much longer than the HML-2 Rec second exon, 62 aa compared to 18 aa, and has only 28% aa identity in the first 18 residues (Figure 6B).
evidence: This is based on sequence comparison shown in Figure 6B.

claim: The HML-8-derived exon of sRec is much longer than the HML-2 Rec second exon (62 aa compared to 18 aa) and has only 28% aa identity in the first 18 residues.
source: The HML-2-derived exon of this Rec-like protein, which we have called sRec, is ~80% identical at the amino acid level to HML-2 Rec; the HML-8-derived exon, in contrast, is much longer than the HML-2 Rec second exon, 62 aa compared to 18 aa, and has only 28% aa identity in the first 18 residues (Figure 6B).
evidence: This is based on sequence comparison shown in Figure 6B.

claim: All three SERV-K/MER11 constructs (MER11U3R, MER11, and MER11-Δenv) showed strong RNA transport activity, both with and without sRec.
source: We found that all three SERV-K/MER11 constructs showed strong RNA transport activity, both with and without sRec (Figure 7B, C, Figure 7—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is based on the dual reporter assay shown in Figure 7.

claim: No increase in RNA transport activity was seen with the addition of sRec.
source: No increase in activity was seen with the addition of sRec, and sRec did not increase transport activity when co-transfected with the RcRe reporter either (Figure 7—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is based on the dual reporter assay shown in Figure 7 and Figure 7—figure supplement 1.

claim: The MER11U3R construct has approximately 2-fold higher eGFP/mCherry ratio than the MER11 construct.
source: The highest eGFP/mCherry ratio was seen with the full-length MER11U3R construct, approximately 2-fold higher than the MER11 construct, which had a signal approximately 15-fold higher than MER11-Δenv.
evidence: This is based on flow cytometry quantification shown in Figure 7C.

claim: The MER11 construct has approximately 15-fold higher eGFP/mCherry ratio than MER11-Δenv.
source: The highest eGFP/mCherry ratio was seen with the full-length MER11U3R construct, approximately 2-fold higher than the MER11 construct, which had a signal approximately 15-fold higher than MER11-Δenv.
evidence: This is based on flow cytometry quantification shown in Figure 7C.

claim: The MER11-Δenv construct has eight times higher activity than the background signal seen with RcRE in the absence of Rec.
source: Although it shows far less RNA transport activity than the other two SERV-K/MER11 constructs, the MER11-Δenv construct has eight times higher activity than the background signal seen with RcRE in the absence of Rec, and also higher activity than the MPMV CTE positive control.
evidence: This is based on flow cytometry quantification shown in Figure 7C.

claim: The MER11-Δenv construct has higher activity than the MPMV CTE positive control.
source: Although it shows far less RNA transport activity than the other two SERV-K/MER11 constructs, the MER11-Δenv construct has eight times higher activity than the background signal seen with RcRE in the absence of Rec, and also higher activity than the MPMV CTE positive control.
evidence: This is based on flow cytometry quantification shown in Figure 7C.

claim: Replacing the MPMV wild-type CTE with the MER11 element restored infectivity to ~70% of wild-type levels.
source: As expected, MPMV with the wtCTE showed strong VSV-G-dependent infectivity, and deleting the wtCTE nearly completely abolished infectivity, despite equal or higher eGFP expression in producer cells. Replacing the wtCTE with a MER11 element restored infectivity to ~70% of wild-type levels.
evidence: This is based on the MPMV infection assay shown in Figure 8.

claim: The SERV-K/MER11 HML-8-derived region is a bona fide CTE capable of functionally replacing the MPMV CTE during viral replication.
source: Thus, the SERV-K/MER11 HML-8-derived region is a bona fide CTE capable of functionally replacing the MPMV CTE during viral replication.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the MPMV infection assay shown in Figure 8.

claim: The recombination resulted in the formation of a chimeric env gene with the SU surface subunit and part of the TM transmembrane subunit derived from HML-2 env and the rest of TM derived from HML-8 env.
source: This recombination resulted in the formation of a chimeric env gene, with the SU surface subunit and part of the TM transmembrane subunit derived from HML-2 env and the rest of TM derived from HML-8 env, including the transmembrane alpha helix and the cytoplasmic tail.
evidence: This is based on sequence analysis.

claim: The majority of the 106 recombinant proviruses are much younger than the oldest insertions.
source: The majority of the 106 recombinant proviruses so far identified in rhesus genomes are much younger, however, including two subclades of rhesus-specific insertions.
evidence: This is based on age estimation analysis shown in Figure 3.

claim: Many young proviruses are insertionally polymorphic and present at low frequencies in macaques.
source: Many of these young proviruses are insertionally polymorphic and present at low frequencies in macaques, and 36 of them have identical LTRs.
evidence: This is based on PCR screening shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1 and LTR analysis.

claim: The evidence suggests infectious activity of HERV-K-like retroviruses in rhesus macaques within the last 500–250,000 years.
source: Taken together, this evidence suggests infectious activity of HERV-K-like retroviruses in rhesus macaques within the last 500–250,000 years, and the potential for ongoing replication.
evidence: This is an inference based on multiple lines of evidence including age estimates, insertional polymorphism, and intact ORFs.

claim: There is potential for ongoing replication of HERV-K-like retroviruses in rhesus macaques.
source: Taken together, this evidence suggests infectious activity of HERV-K-like retroviruses in rhesus macaques within the last 500–250,000 years, and the potential for ongoing replication.
evidence: This is speculation based on the young age of some proviruses.

claim: Two proviruses have intact ORFs for the full gag-pro-pol region and could thus potentially make functional retroviral cores.
source: We investigated the coding capacity of these proviruses, and identified full-length ORFs for all genes, including 28 gag, 13 pro, 6 pol, and 7 env ORFs; two proviruses have intact ORFs for the full gag-pro-pol region and could thus potentially make functional retroviral cores, although they are lacking env, and so could not make infectious virus without complementation in trans from a provirus encoding a functional env gene.
evidence: This is an inference based on the presence of intact gag-pro-pol ORFs.

claim: The two proviruses with intact gag-pro-pol could not make infectious virus without complementation in trans from a provirus encoding a functional env gene.
source: We investigated the coding capacity of these proviruses, and identified full-length ORFs for all genes, including 28 gag, 13 pro, 6 pol, and 7 env ORFs; two proviruses have intact ORFs for the full gag-pro-pol region and could thus potentially make functional retroviral cores, although they are lacking env, and so could not make infectious virus without complementation in trans from a provirus encoding a functional env gene.
evidence: This is an inference based on the absence of intact env ORFs in these proviruses.

claim: The overall nucleotide sequence identity of the coding region between consensus recent SERV-K/MER11 and HERV-Kcon is 89.2%.
source: We compared the sequence of the consensus recent SERV-K/MER11 to HERV-Kcon; the overall nucleotide sequence identity of the coding region is 89.2% and amino acid identity of Gag, Pro, Pol, and Env are 78.5, 91, 91, and 82.5%, respectively.
evidence: This is based on sequence comparison analysis.

claim: The amino acid identity of Gag, Pro, Pol, and Env between consensus recent SERV-K/MER11 and HERV-Kcon are 78.5, 91, 91, and 82.5%, respectively.
source: We compared the sequence of the consensus recent SERV-K/MER11 to HERV-Kcon; the overall nucleotide sequence identity of the coding region is 89.2% and amino acid identity of Gag, Pro, Pol, and Env are 78.5, 91, 91, and 82.5%, respectively.
evidence: This is based on sequence comparison analysis.

claim: Many of the basic features of HML-2 biology are likely conserved between SERV-K/MER11 and human HML-2.
source: Although the sequence of these viruses has diverged, as expected for RNA viruses that have evolved separately for over 20 million years, it is likely that many of the basic features of HML-2 biology are conserved between these two viruses.
evidence: This is an inference based on sequence similarity.

claim: The deletion-containing proviruses are presumably not replication competent.
source: Although many of the proviruses characterized have one or more full-length ORFs, the majority of the proviruses also contain large shared deletions in the coding regions. The deletion containing proviruses are presumably not replication competent, and are reminiscent of human Type 1 HML-2s (Löwer et al., 1993), which contain a 292-bp env deletion, and other shared deletions observed in gorilla HML-2s (Holloway et al., 2019).
evidence: This is an inference based on the presence of large deletions in coding regions.

claim: The shared deletions in SERV-K/MER11 are likely propagated via co-packaging with replication competent viral genomes.
source: The deletion containing proviruses are presumably not replication competent, and are reminiscent of human Type 1 HML-2s (Löwer et al., 1993), which contain a 292-bp env deletion, and other shared deletions observed in gorilla HML-2s (Holloway et al., 2019). Like those deletions, they are likely propagated via co-packaging with replication competent viral genomes.
evidence: This is an inference based on comparison to similar deletions in human and gorilla HML-2s.

claim: The LTRs of SERV-K/MER11 have undergone major structural changes with large deletions in the U3 region.
source: In contrast to the coding regions, the LTRs of SERV-K/MER11 have undergone major structural changes, with large deletions in the U3 region.
evidence: This is based on structural analysis shown in Figure 1C and Figure 5C.

claim: The U3 deletions have accumulated over millions of years, with unique deletions appearing in the viral lineages in different host species.
source: These deletions have accumulated over millions of years, with unique deletions appearing in the viral lineages in different host species, all converging on the same region of U3.
evidence: This is based on phylogenetic and structural analysis shown in Figure 3A and Figure 5C.

claim: The majority of the U3 deletions overlap with the RcRE in human HML-2.
